warmup.text: The novel is finished. Today you read two real sources from the years of the Choctaw removal: part of a treaty, and part of a letter by a Choctaw chief. Ask of each one: who wrote this, when, and why?

words.text: Put the history words to work: primary source, secondary source, perspective, bias. Then practice naming your source before every claim. In the game, look for the part that can stand alone as a word.

reading.text: Read the two sources slowly. They are short, and the plain words under each one will help. Keep the story and the record apart: the novel says eighteen thirty, and the treaty sets the removal for eighteen thirty-one to eighteen thirty-three.

assignment.text: Three questions about the novel and the sources. Then revise your draft with the checklist: formal style, two source transitions, a claim with evidence and reasoning, and every fact tied to its source.

game.title: Ears of Corn
game.sub: This week's word game · 3 words today
game.look: Each long word is an ear of corn, like the corn the families cook in Chapter 29. The parts added to the front or the end are the husks. Tap each husk to peel it away. The base word is the ear inside.

do: Read the long word.
Find the part that can stand alone as a word. Leave it.
Tap each part added to the front or the end.
Tap Next word.
how.why: Long words in history writing are short words with parts added. Find the base and you can read and spell the rest.

game.doneLine: Come back tomorrow for three more words.

ears.means: in a way that is not fair or right.

ears.why: en- means in, and -ment makes a noun.
ears.means: a place where people have set up camp.

ears.why: -er makes a person who leads, and -ship makes a noun. Two husks at the end.

art.title: Louisiana Indians Walking Along a Bayou
art.alt: A painting of a family walking in a line beside a bayou under tall trees: a man with a long gun, a child, and two women carrying loads on their backs.
art.look: Alfred Boisseau painted this family in Louisiana in 1847. They are believed to be Choctaw. This is not the Trail of Tears: it was painted about fifteen years later, and some Choctaw families stayed in Mississippi and Louisiana. It is one of very few paintings of Choctaw people made in those years by someone who saw them.

virtue.name: courage
virtue.title: The courage meter
virtue.intro: Think about one moment from real history, in Source B.
virtue.moment: George W. Harkins, a real Choctaw chief, wrote in 1831: “my people are dear to me, with them I must go.” He wrote that he could not stay behind and leave them to struggle alone.
virtue.ask: How much courage did Harkins show? Slide to show.
virtue.take: Mason's take: a great deal. He chose a hard road so his people would not walk it without him.
